blocks.text: His face was strongly shaped, very strongly shaped, like an eagle's. His thin nose had a high bridge, and his nostrils curved in a strange way. He had a high, rounded forehead. His hair grew thinly near the sides of his forehead, but very thickly everywhere else. His eyebrows were very large and almost met above his nose. Their thick hair seemed to curl because there was so much of it. As far as I could see under his heavy moustache, his mouth was hard and rather cruel-looking. He had unusually sharp white teeth. They stuck out over his lips. His lips were remarkably red, which showed amazing life and energy in a man of his age. As for the rest, his ears were pale and extremely pointed at the tops. His chin was broad and strong, and his cheeks were firm, though thin. The general effect was that his face was extraordinarily pale.

Until now, I had only noticed the backs of his hands as they lay on his knees in the firelight. They had seemed rather white and fine. Now I saw them close to me, and I could not help noticing that they were rather rough. They were broad, with short, thick fingers. Strange to say, there were hairs in the middle of the palm. The nails were long and thin, and cut to a sharp point. The Count leaned over me, and his hands touched me. I could not hold back a sudden shake of fear and disgust. Perhaps his breath smelled bad, for a horrible feeling of sickness came over me. No matter what I tried to do, I could not hide it. The Count clearly noticed this and pulled back. He gave a grim sort of smile, which showed his sticking-out teeth more than before. Then he sat down again on his own side of the fireplace. We were both silent for a while. I looked towards the window and saw the first faint line of the coming dawn. A strange quiet seemed to lie over everything. But as I listened, I heard the howling of many wolves, as if from down below in the valley. The Count’s eyes shone, and he said:
“Listen to them—the children of the night. What music they make!” I suppose he saw some expression on my face that seemed strange to him, so he added:
“Ah, sir, you people who live in the city cannot share the feelings of the hunter.” Then he stood up and said:

“But you must be tired. Your bedroom is all ready, and tomorrow you can sleep as late as you like. I have to be away until the afternoon, so sleep well and dream well!” With a polite bow, he opened the door to the eight-sided room for me himself, and I went into my bedroom....

I feel as if I am lost in a sea of strange wonders. I have doubts, and I am afraid. I think strange things, which I do not dare to admit even to myself. May God protect me, if only for the sake of the people I love!

7 May.—It is early morning again, but I have rested and enjoyed the last twenty-four hours. I slept until late in the day and woke up naturally by myself. After I got dressed, I went into the room where we had eaten supper. I found a cold breakfast set out on the table. The coffee was kept hot because the pot stood on the floor by the fireplace. There was a card on the table, with these words written on it:

“I have to be away for a while. Do not wait for me.—D.” I began to eat and enjoyed a big meal. When I finished, I looked for a bell so that I could let the servants know I was done. However, I could not find one. Some things are certainly missing in a strange way in this house, especially when I look at the extraordinary signs of wealth all around me. The dishes and spoons on the table are made of gold. They are so beautifully made that they must be worth a huge amount of money. The curtains, the cloth covering the chairs and sofas, and the curtains around my bed are made of the most expensive and beautiful fabrics. They must have been worth an amazing amount when they were made. They are hundreds of years old, yet they are in excellent condition. I saw fabrics like them at Hampton Court, but there they were worn out, damaged at the edges, and full of holes made by moths. Still, there is not a mirror in any of the rooms. There is not even a small dressing-table mirror on my table. I had to take the little shaving mirror from my bag before I could shave or brush my hair. I have not seen a servant anywhere yet, and I have not heard a sound near the castle except the howling of wolves. My meal was between five and six o’clock, so I do not know whether to call it breakfast or dinner. Some time after I finished it, I looked around for something to read. I did not want to walk around the castle until I had asked the Count if I could. There was nothing at all to read or write with in the room—no book, no newspaper, not even paper and pens. So I opened another door in the room and found a kind of library. I tried the door opposite mine, but I found that it was locked.
